Respiration means the process of breathing — specifically, the complete cycle of drawing air into your body and then pushing it back out. One full cycle of breathing in (inhaling) and breathing out (exhaling) is one act of respiration.

When you say "respiration," you're not just describing a single breath; you're referring to the ongoing biological process that keeps a living organism alive by continuously exchanging gases between the body and its environment.

When you breathe in, your lungs pull in oxygen from the surrounding air. Your blood then carries that oxygen to every cell in your body. At the same time, your body's cells are constantly producing a waste gas called carbon dioxide. That carbon dioxide travels back through your blood to your lungs, and when you breathe out, it leaves your body.

So respiration is essentially a two-way gas exchange:

  • Oxygen in → goes to body's cells
  • Carbon dioxide out → expelled from body

This is sometimes called external respiration or pulmonary respiration, because it involves the lungs and the outside environment.
The Deeper Biological Meaning: Cellular Respiration

Here is where the word gets richer and more important. In biology, "respiration" also refers to something happening inside your cells — something you cannot see or feel, but which is the real reason you need to breathe at all.

Your body needs energy to do everything — to move, to think, to heal, to grow. This energy comes from food (specifically from a sugar called glucose). But your body cannot use glucose directly as fuel. It has to convert it into a usable form of energy. This conversion process is called cellular respiration.

Think of it like this: glucose is like raw wood, and your cells need electricity, not wood. Cellular respiration is the "power plant" inside each cell that burns the wood (glucose) and produces electricity (energy), along with some exhaust (carbon dioxide and water).

The full equation in plain words: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water

This is why breathing is so essential — your cells need the oxygen you breathe in to carry out this conversion process. Without oxygen, the conversion cannot happen efficiently, and your cells begin to die.

1. Aerobic Respiration (with oxygen)

This is the standard, highly efficient form of respiration that your body uses most of the time. Because oxygen is present, glucose is broken down completely, releasing a large amount of energy. The byproducts — carbon dioxide and water — are harmless and easily expelled.

This is what your body does when you're at rest, walking, or doing light activity.

2. Anaerobic Respiration (without oxygen)

Sometimes your muscles need energy faster than oxygen can be delivered — like during a sprint or intense exercise. In these situations, your cells can still produce energy without oxygen, but the process is far less efficient and produces a byproduct called lactic acid.

That burning sensation in your muscles after intense exercise? That's largely the result of lactic acid building up — a telltale sign of anaerobic respiration at work.

Anaerobic respiration is a short-term emergency solution. It cannot sustain a cell for long, and the body must eventually "pay back" the oxygen debt by breathing harder after the exertion.
How the Two Meanings Are Connected

Here's the elegant link: breathing (the outer process) exists to serve cellular respiration (the inner process).

You breathe — in and out, in and out — purely so that:

  1. Oxygen can reach your cells to fuel cellular respiration.
  2. The carbon dioxide produced by cellular respiration can be removed from your body.

If you stop breathing, cellular respiration in your cells eventually halts, energy production stops, and life ceases. This is why respiration, in both its senses, is considered one of the fundamental characteristics of all living things.

It's worth knowing that respiration isn't unique to humans or even to animals. Every living organism respires — plants, fungi, bacteria, and all animals. Plants are famous for photosynthesis (making their own food using sunlight), but they also carry out cellular respiration, just like animals, to convert that food into usable energy.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

• "The doctor monitored the patient's respiration after surgery to ensure the lungs were functioning well." → Here it means the act of breathing.
  • "Cellular respiration is the process by which cells convert glucose into energy." → Here it refers to the biochemical process inside cells.
  • "At high altitudes, respiration becomes more difficult because the air contains less oxygen." → Refers to breathing.
  • "Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces alcohol as a byproduct — the same process used in brewing beer." → Biological process without oxygen.

In short: Respiration means breathing at the surface level — the continuous in-and-out movement of air through your lungs. But at its deeper biological core, respiration is the entire life-sustaining system by which living organisms extract energy from food using oxygen. The breathing you do every moment of your life is simply the visible, physical part of this deeper, invisible process happening inside every single one of your trillions of cells, every second, for as long as you live.
